15.01.title: The design process and decision matrices
15.01.html:
Machine design is not one calculation. It is a loop: define the need, generate several concepts, select one, analyse it in detail, test, and go round again when something fails. Phase 15 is about the analysis tools for the machine elements every product is built from: shafts, bearings, gears, bolts, springs. Before any of that, though, someone has to pick the concept, and that choice is usually made with a weighted decision matrix.

The weighted decision matrix

List the criteria that matter, give each an importance weight wj​, and score every concept i against every criterion on the same scale (here 1 = poor to 5 = excellent). Normalise the weights so they sum to one, then

Ti​=j∑​w^j​sij​,w^j​=∑k​wk​wj​​.

The concept with the highest total wins. Two properties make this useful and also show its limits:

  1. Only the ratios of the weights matter. Multiplying every weight by 7 changes nothing, because of the normalisation.
  2. Totals are linear in the weights. If you raise one weight w^j​ from 0 to 1 while scaling the others down in proportion, each total moves along a straight line, so the point where two concepts swap is a single linear equation. That is a sensitivity check: if a small change in a weight flips the winner, the matrix has not really decided anything.

The scores are judgements, not measurements. The matrix makes those judgements explicit and easy to argue about, which is its real value.

Worked exampleChoosing a drivetrain for a commuter bike

Four concepts are scored on cost, mass, efficiency, maintenance and gear range:

Concept Cost Mass Efficiency Maintenance Gear range
1x derailleur 4 5 5 2 4
8-speed hub 3 2 3 4 3
belt + hub 1 2 3 5 3
single speed 5 5 5 4 1

A commuter in a wet, flat city gives importance points 25, 20, 15, 30, 10 (out of 100), so the weights are 0.25, 0.20, 0.15, 0.30, 0.10.

  1. Single speed: 0.25⋅5+0.20⋅5+0.15⋅5+0.30⋅4+0.10⋅1=4.30.
  2. 1x derailleur 3.75, 8-speed hub 3.10, belt + hub 2.90. Single speed wins.
  3. Sensitivity: move to a hilly town and raise the gear-range weight λ, scaling the other four in proportion. With λ=0 the totals are 4.667 (single speed) and 3.722 (derailleur); with λ=1 they are 1 and 4. They cross where 0.944=3.944λ, so λ=17/71=0.2394. Above about 24% weight on gear range, the derailleur wins.

Exercise 1Doubling the cost weight

Show step-by-step solution

  2. Single speed: 0.5⋅5+0.2⋅5+0.1⋅5+0.1⋅4+0.1⋅1=4.50.
  3. Belt + hub: 0.5⋅1+0.2⋅2+0.1⋅3+0.1⋅5+0.1⋅3=2.00.
  4. The 1x derailleur gets 2+1+0.5+0.2+0.4=4.10. Single speed still wins, by a wider margin.

15.02.title: Safety factors and reliability
15.02.html:
A safety factor is the ratio of strength to stress, n=R/S. Codes give values such as 1.5 or 2, and for a part with well-known loads and material that is fine. But strength and stress are both scattered: one batch of aluminium is stronger than the next, and one rider hits a pothole harder than another. Two designs with the same safety factor can have very different chances of failing. Stress-strength interference puts a number on that chance.

Two overlapping distributions

Model strength R and stress S as independent normal variables with means μR​,μS​ and standard deviations σR​,σS​. The part fails when R<S, that is when the margin M=R−S is negative. A difference of independent normals is normal, with

μM​=μR​−μS​,σM​=σR2​+σS2​​.

So the probability of failure is

Pf​=P(M<0)=Φ(−z),z=σR2​+σS2​​μR​−μS​​,

where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution and z is the reliability index. The central safety factor μR​/μS​ does not appear on its own: scatter matters as much as the mean margin.

Monte Carlo checks this without any formula: draw a few million (R,S) pairs and count how often R<S. The count has a binomial standard error Pf​(1−Pf​)/N​, and the estimate should land within a few of those of Φ(−z).

Assumptions: normal distributions, independence, and a single failure mode. Real strength data has a lower tail that is often thinner than normal (materials are proof-tested), and loads often have a fatter one, so for very small Pf​ the tails matter more than the formula suggests.

Worked exampleAn aluminium handlebar clamp

Strength 300 MPa with 8% scatter (σR​=24 MPa); peak stress in use 180 MPa with 15% scatter (σS​=27 MPa).

  1. Central safety factor 300/180=1.667.
  2. z=120/242+272​=120/36.12=3.3218, so Pf​=Φ(−3.3218)=4.47×10−4: about 1 clamp in 2240.
  3. Two million Monte Carlo pairs give 4.68×10−4±0.15×10−4, within 1.4 standard errors.
  4. Double both scatters, keep the means: the safety factor is still 1.667, but z=1.661 and Pf​=0.0484, about 1 in 21.
  5. For Pf​=10−6 we need z=4.7534. With strength scatter fixed at 8% of its mean, the mean strength must be 370.6 MPa, a safety factor of 2.06.

Exercise 1A heavier rider

In the clamp example the mean stress rises to 200 MPa, everything else unchanged. Find z and Pf​.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. z=(300−200)/36.12=2.768.
  2. Pf​=Φ(−2.768)=2.82×10−3, about 1 in 355.
  3. An 11% rise in load raised the failure probability more than sixfold. That steep tail is why reliability targets need margin.

15.03.title: Tolerances, fits and stack-ups
15.03.html:
No part is made exactly to size. A drawing that says “25 mm” really means “25 mm give or take something”, and the designer chooses that something. Choose it too tight and the part is expensive; too loose and the bearing rattles or the gear will not press on. This lesson covers the two everyday tools: ISO fits for a shaft in a hole, and stack-up analysis for a chain of parts.

ISO 286 fits

The tolerance grade IT sets the width of the band. ISO 286 builds it from a tolerance unit that grows slowly with size D (the geometric mean of a size step, in mm):

i=0.45D1/3+0.001D  μm,IT6=10i,  IT7=16i,  IT8=25i.

A letter sets the position of the band. In the common basic-hole system the hole is always H (lower deviation zero) and the shaft letter does the work: g sits below zero (clearance), h touches zero, k and n sit above zero (transition), p and s higher still (interference). The fundamental deviations also come from formulas, for example es​=−2.5D0.34 for g, ei​=0.6D1/3 for k and ei​=5D0.34 for n (μm), rounded to whole micrometres.

A fit is then described by its extreme clearances:

cmax​=holemax​−shaftmin​,cmin​=holemin​−shaftmax​.

Both positive: a clearance fit. Both negative: an interference fit. One of each: a transition fit, which may go together loose or tight.

Stack-ups: worst case and root-sum-square

When parts sit end to end, their tolerances add. If a gap is g=∑k​sk​Lk​ with signs sk​=±1 and part tolerances ±tk​:

tWC​=k∑​tk​,tRSS​=∑k​tk2​​≤tWC​.

Worst case guarantees assembly even if every part is at its limit in the bad direction. Root-sum-square assumes the errors are independent and each tolerance is 3σ of a normal distribution; then the gap’s standard deviation is tRSS​/3 and 99.73% of assemblies land inside ±tRSS​. With many parts, RSS is much narrower, because it is unlikely that all parts are off in the same direction at once.

Worked exampleA 25 mm bearing seat and a bike hub stack

  1. For 25 mm the size step is 18 to 30 mm, so D=18⋅30​=23.24 and i=1.308 μm. IT6 = 13 μm and IT7 = 21 μm, the table values.
  2. 25 H7/g6: hole 0 to +21 μm; shaft es​=−2.5⋅23.240.34=−7, so −7 to −20 μm. Clearance from +7 to +41 μm: a sliding fit.
  3. 25 H7/k6: shaft +2 to +15 μm, so from 15 μm interference to 19 μm clearance: a transition fit, typical for a bearing inner ring that must be located but still removable.
  4. A hub stack: housing 50.30 ± 0.10 mm minus two bearings 15.00 ± 0.05 and a spacer 20.00 ± 0.08. Nominal play 0.30 mm. Worst case ± 0.280 mm; RSS 0.12+0.052+0.082+0.052​=±0.146 mm.
  5. A million Monte Carlo assemblies (each tolerance = 3σ) give a play standard deviation of 0.0487 mm, equal to RSS/3, and 0.27% outside the RSS band, as predicted.

Exercise 1A 50 mm shaft

For a 50 mm diameter (size step 30 to 50 mm), compute IT7 and the g6 shaft limits, and the clearance range of 50 H7/g6.

  1. D=30⋅50​=38.73, i=0.45⋅38.731/3+0.0387=1.561 μm.
  2. IT7 = 16i=25 μm; IT6 = 10i=16 μm.
  3. g: es​=−2.5⋅38.730.34=−8.66→−9 μm, so the shaft is −9 to −25 μm.
  4. Clearance from 0−(−9)=9 μm to 25−(−25)=50 μm.

15.04.title: Shaft design for fatigue
15.04.html:
A rotating shaft carrying a gear sees its bending stress go from tension to compression once per revolution, millions of times. So a shaft is almost always designed for fatigue, not for a single static load. The standard recipe combines the bending moment diagram, stress concentration, the Marin endurance limit and the Goodman line into one diameter formula.

Loads on a rotating shaft

For a shaft supported in two bearings with point loads, statics gives the reactions and the bending moment M(x), which peaks under a load. Because the shaft rotates while the load direction stays fixed in space, a fibre on the surface sees fully reversed bending: alternating moment Ma​=M, mean Mm​=0. The torque from the gear is usually steady: Tm​=T, Ta​=0.

The DE-Goodman diameter

Combine bending and torsion with the distortion-energy (von Mises) equivalent stress, apply the fatigue stress concentration factors Kf​ (bending) and Kfs​ (torsion) at the shoulder, and put the alternating and mean parts on the Goodman line σa′​/Se​+σm′​/Sut​=1/n. Solving for d:

d=[π16n​(Se​4(Kf​Ma​)2+3(Kfs​Ta​)2​​+Sut​4(Kf​Mm​)2+3(Kfs​Tm​)2​​)]1/3.

The endurance limit itself depends on the diameter through the size factor kb​=1.24d−0.107 (for 2.8 to 51 mm), with Se​=ka​kb​0.5Sut​ and the machined-surface factor ka​=4.51Sut−0.265​. So the formula is solved by fixed-point iteration: guess d, compute Se​, compute a new d, repeat. It converges in a handful of steps because kb​ varies slowly.

Assumptions: steady torque, fully reversed bending, a single critical section, Goodman (slightly conservative compared with test data), and Kf​ values taken as given. In a real design you check every shoulder and keyway, and the deflection and critical speed too.

Worked exampleA gearbox countershaft

Bearings 300 mm apart; a gear force of 2000 N at 100 mm and a pulley pull of 1200 N at 220 mm, both in the same plane. Steady torque 150 N·m. 1045 cold-drawn steel, Sut​=630 MPa; shoulder Kf​=1.7, Kfs​=1.5; target n=2.

  1. Reactions: R2​=(2000⋅100+1200⋅220)/300=1546.7 N, R1​=1653.3 N.
  2. Peak moment under the gear: M=1653.3⋅0.1=165.33 N·m (at the pulley it is 1546.7⋅0.08=123.7 N·m).
  3. ka​=4.51⋅630−0.265=0.817. After iterating, d=31.84 mm, kb​=0.856, Se​=220.4 MPa.
  4. Bending term 2⋅1.7⋅165333/220.4=2550.2; torsion term 3​⋅1.5⋅150000/630=618.6. Then d=[10.186⋅3168.8]1/3=31.84 mm.
  5. Back-check: σa′​=88.70 MPa, σm′​=61.49 MPa, and 1/(88.70/220.4+61.49/630)=2.000.
  6. For n = 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3 the diameter is 28.85, 31.84, 34.37, 36.59 mm: a larger safety factor always needs a larger shaft, roughly as n1/3. A designer would pick the next standard size, 32 or 35 mm.

Exercise 1Without the torque

If the same shaft carried the bending loads but no torque, what diameter would n=2 need? And with 50% more bending moment and the torque back?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. With T=0 only the bending term remains; iterating gives d=29.54 mm.
  2. With M=248.0 N·m and T=150 N·m, d=35.77 mm.
  3. The bending term dominates: dropping all the torque saves only 2.3 mm, while 50% more bending adds 3.9 mm.

15.05.title: Keys, splines and press fits
15.05.html:
A gear on a shaft has to pass torque without slipping. There are three classic ways: a key in a slot, a spline (many keys machined into the shaft), or a press fit, where the hub bore is made slightly smaller than the shaft and friction does the work. The press fit has no slot to weaken the shaft, but its capacity depends entirely on the contact pressure, and that comes from thick-cylinder elasticity.

Keys and splines

A parallel key of width w, height h and length L on a shaft of diameter d carries the force F=2T/d at the shaft surface. Two checks:

τ=dwL2T​  (shear across the key),σc​=dhL4T​  (crushing on half the key height).

For a square key (w=h) the crushing stress is twice the shear stress. The key is meant to be the weak link: it is cheap to replace, and it protects the shaft and hub. A spline spreads the same torque over many teeth, so it is shorter for the same torque and lets a hub slide axially, as on a gearbox selector or a bike’s freehub body.

Press fits from Lamé

A hub (bore R, outer radius ro​) is forced onto a solid shaft of radius R+δ, where δ is the radial interference. Both parts are thick cylinders. Lamé's solution gives the radial displacement of each under the interface pressure p; the hub bore must grow and the shaft shrink by a total of δ:

δ=pR[Eo​1​(ro2​−R2ro2​+R2​+νo​)+Ei​1​(1−νi​)].

For the same material on both sides this simplifies to

p=2Rro2​Eδ(ro2​−R2)​.

Friction then gives the torque and axial capacity, and the hub bore carries the largest hoop stress:

T=2πR2Lμp,Faxial​=2πRLμp,σt,bore​=pro2​−R2ro2​+R2​.

Assumptions: plane stress, both parts elastic, hub length equal to the fit length, and a friction coefficient around 0.1 to 0.2 for dry steel (it varies a lot, so press fits are rated conservatively). The code checks Lamé against an independent finite-difference solution of the radial displacement equation u′′+u′/r−u/r2=0.

Worked exampleA scooter gear pressed on a 20 mm shaft

Steel hub, outer diameter 60 mm, length 25 mm, on a 20 mm steel shaft; diametral interference 20 μm (radial δ=0.010 mm); E=207 GPa, μ=0.15.

  1. p=207000⋅0.010⋅(900−100)/(2⋅10⋅900)=92.0 MPa. The finite-difference solution agrees to better than 0.01%.
  2. Torque capacity T=2π⋅102⋅25⋅0.15⋅92.0=216.8 N·m; push-out force 21.68 kN.
  3. Hoop stress at the hub bore: 92.0⋅1000/800=115.0 MPa, comfortably elastic for steel.
  4. A 6 × 6 mm key, 25 mm long, carrying 100 N·m instead: shear 2⋅100000/(20⋅6⋅25)=66.7 MPa, crushing 133.3 MPa.

The same hub uses a 20 H7/s6 fit. From the ISO tables, the hole is 0 to +21 μm and the s6 shaft is +35 to +48 μm. Find the range of contact pressure and torque capacity, and the largest hub hoop stress.

  1. Diametral interference from 35−21=14 μm to 48−0=48 μm, so radial 7 to 24 μm.
  2. p=207000⋅800/18000⋅δ=9200δ: from 64.4 to 220.8 MPa.
  3. Torque from 151.7 N·m (loosest) to 520.2 N·m (tightest). Design on the loosest: 151.7 N·m.
  4. Largest hoop stress 220.8⋅1.25=276.0 MPa, still below the yield strength of a medium-carbon steel hub, but worth checking.

15.06.title: Rolling bearings and fatigue life
15.06.html:
A ball bearing does not wear out like a brake pad. If it is clean and lubricated, it fails by rolling contact fatigue: after many millions of stress cycles, a crack starts below the surface of a race and a flake of metal spalls out. The time to that event is random, even for identical bearings under identical loads, so bearing life is a statistical quantity.

The L10 life

The basic rating life L10​ is the number of revolutions that 90% of a large group of identical bearings survive. Tests show it follows a power law in the load:

L10​=(PC​)a million revolutions,a=3 (ball),a=310​ (roller).

C is the dynamic load rating from the catalogue: the load giving L10​ = one million revolutions. P is the equivalent load. For combined radial and axial load the catalogue gives P=XFr​+YFa​, with X and Y depending on the ratio Fa​/Fr​ and the bearing type. Because of the cube law, doubling the load cuts a ball bearing’s life by 8, and a 10% overload costs about 25% of the life.

Rearranged for selection: Creq​=PL1/a, with L in millions of revolutions.

Other reliabilities

Fatigue lives scatter roughly as a Weibull distribution: the fraction surviving to life L is exp[−(L/η)b], with slope b≈1.5 for ball bearings. Anchoring it at the L10​ point gives the life at any reliability R:

LR​=L10​(ln(1/0.9)ln(1/R)​)1/b.

So 95% reliability gives 0.62L10​, 99% gives 0.21L10​, and the median bearing lasts 3.5L10​. (ISO 281 tabulates slightly different factors, 0.64 and 0.25, because it adds a minimum life below which no bearing fails.)

Worked exampleA scooter wheel bearing

A 6202 deep groove ball bearing has C=8060 N. On a scooter wheel of 450 mm diameter it carries an equivalent load of 1500 N (weight plus a dynamic allowance).

  1. L10​=(8060/1500)3=155.1 million revolutions. The wheel rolls 1.414 m per revolution, so that is about 219 000 km.
  2. At 3000 N: 155.1/8=19.4 million revolutions.
  3. Combined load Fr​=1200 N, Fa​=400 N with catalogue factors X=0.56, Y=1.8: P=672+720=1392 N, L10​=194.1 million revolutions.
  4. At 95% reliability the life is 0.619L10​=96.0 million revolutions.
  5. A simulated fleet of 200 000 bearings with Weibull lives: 10.01% fail before L10​, and the median is 3.51L10​, as the formula says.

The fatigue life is huge, yet scooter wheel bearings in Bali often last only a few years. Real bearings in wet, sandy service fail from contamination and corrosion long before fatigue; the catalogue’s life modification factors (ISO 281 aISO​) can cut the life tenfold or more for dirty conditions. Seals matter more than C here.

Exercise 1Choosing a bearing

A gearbox shaft runs at 1500 rpm with an equivalent radial load of 2.2 kN, and must reach 20 000 hours with 90% reliability. What dynamic rating is needed for a ball bearing and for a roller bearing?

  2. Ball: C=2200⋅18001/3=2200⋅12.164=26760 N, so about 26.8 kN (a 6306 has 33.2 kN, enough).
  3. Roller: C=2200⋅18000.3=2200⋅9.475=20850 N, about 20.8 kN.

15.07.title: Plain bearings and the Reynolds equation
15.07.html:
A car engine’s crankshaft does not run on balls. It runs on plain bearings: smooth shells with a film of oil a few hundredths of a millimetre thick. When the shaft turns, it drags oil into a narrowing gap, the oil pressure rises, and the shaft floats with no metal contact at all. This is hydrodynamic lubrication, and its governing equation was written down by Osborne Reynolds in 1886.

The Reynolds equation

In a thin film the flow is viscous and nearly parallel to the surfaces (Phase 12 met this as lubrication theory). Integrating the Navier-Stokes equations across the film thickness h(x), and asking that the flow rate be the same at every x, gives the one-dimensional Reynolds equation for a surface sliding at speed U over a stationary one:

dxd​(h3dxdp​)=6μUdxdh​,p(0)=p(L)=0.

The right-hand side is the source of pressure. If h is constant, dh/dx=0 and there is no pressure: parallel surfaces carry no load. If the gap narrows in the direction of motion, oil is squeezed into a wedge and the pressure rises.

For a plane pad tapering from hin​ to hout​, with K=hin​/hout​, the load per unit width has a closed form:

W′=hout2​(K−1)26μUL2​[lnK−K+12(K−1)​].

The bracket is positive only for K>1 (converging). It peaks at K≈2.2, where W′hout2​/(μUL2)=0.160. A diverging film predicts suction, which real oil cannot sustain: it cavitates, so the diverging part simply carries nothing.

The load grows with viscosity and speed and falls with the square of the film thickness. Turn that around: for a given load, a faster or more viscous film floats higher. That is why a bearing that starts and stops under load (with U→0) is where wear happens.

Assumptions: an infinitely wide pad (no side leakage), constant viscosity, rigid surfaces. A square pad loses roughly half its load through the sides; real design uses 2D charts or numerical solutions.

Worked exampleA tilting-pad thrust bearing

One pad: length 50 mm in the sliding direction, surface speed 10 m/s, hot SAE 30 oil μ=0.03 Pa·s, minimum film 20 μm, taper K=2.2.

  1. Finite differences on 2001 points give a peak pressure of 9.588 MPa and a load of 300.45 kN per metre of width, the same as the closed form to five figures.
  2. For a 50 mm wide pad that is about 15.0 kN, before the side-leakage correction.
  3. With a parallel film (K=1) the load is zero; with a diverging film the solver gives a minimum of −37.5 MPa of suction, which cavitates in practice.
  4. Double the speed to 20 m/s: the load doubles to 600.9 kN/m. Double the film to 40 μm at the same speed: the load falls by 4 to 75.1 kN/m.

Exercise 1A different taper

For the same pad, what is the load per metre width for K=1.5 and for K=3? Why is the best taper a compromise?

  1. Use W′=6μUL2/(hout2​(K−1)2)[lnK−2(K−1)/(K+1)] with 6μUL2/hout2​=6⋅0.03⋅10⋅0.0025/(4×10−10)=1.125×107 N/m.
  2. K=1.5: bracket 0.405465−0.4=0.005465, divided by 0.25: 245.9 kN/m.
  3. K=3: bracket 1.098612−1=0.098612, divided by 4: 277.3 kN/m.
  4. A small taper builds little pressure; a large taper lets most of the oil flow back out of the wide inlet. The optimum, K≈2.2, gives 300.4 kN/m.

15.08.title: Gear geometry and the involute
15.08.html:
Two gears must turn at a constant speed ratio, or the drive would shudder twice per tooth. That is a strong geometric condition on the tooth shape, called conjugate action: the common normal at the contact point must always pass through the same point on the line of centres, the pitch point. Almost every power gear in the world meets it with one curve, the involute of a circle.

The involute

Unwind a taut string from a circle of radius rb​ (the base circle). The end of the string traces the involute. With roll angle t:

x=rb​(cost+tsint),y=rb​(sint−tcost).

The string is always tangent to the base circle and perpendicular to the curve, so the normal to an involute is tangent to its base circle. Put two gears side by side: the common tangent to their two base circles is a fixed straight line, the line of action. Both tooth normals must lie along it, so the contact point slides along it, and it crosses the line of centres at a fixed pitch point. The speed ratio is constant:

ω1​ω2​​=rb2​rb1​​=z2​z1​​.

The line of action makes the pressure angle ϕ (usually 20°) with the pitch-line tangent, and rb​=rcosϕ. A bonus: changing the centre distance slightly changes ϕ but not the ratio, so involute gears tolerate mounting errors.

Sizes and contact ratio

With module m (mm per tooth of pitch diameter): pitch radius r=mz/2, addendum (tip) radius ra​=r+m, root radius rf​=r−1.25m, circular pitch πm, base pitch pb​=πmcosϕ. The contact ratio is the average number of tooth pairs in contact:

ε=πmcosϕra12​−rb12​​+ra22​−rb22​​−asinϕ​.

It should be at least 1.2 for smooth running. The tooth thickness at radius r′ follows from the involute function invϕ=tanϕ−ϕ: s′=2r′[π/(2z)+invϕ−invϕ′] with cosϕ′=rb​/r′. Pinions with fewer than about 2/sin2ϕ≈17 teeth get undercut by the cutting tool unless the profile is shifted.

Swiss watches are the famous exception: their gear trains use cycloidal teeth, which suit tiny pinions with 6 to 8 leaves and transmit almost no power. Their ratio is not perfectly constant, and nobody notices because the escapement controls the speed.

Worked exampleAn 18 : 45 gear pair

Module 2 mm, pressure angle 20°, z1​=18, z2​=45.

  1. Pitch radii 18 and 45 mm, centre distance 63 mm; base radii 18cos20°=16.9145 and 42.2862 mm.
  2. The code turns the pinion through ±0.15 rad, finds the contact point by bisection on the rotated involute, and checks that both flank normals lie along the line of action. The gear angle it then needs changes at a ratio of exactly 0.400000000 = 18/45 at every step.
  3. Length of action 202−16.91452​+472−42.28622​−63sin20°=9.6405 mm; base pitch 5.9043 mm; contact ratio 1.633. Between one and two tooth pairs carry the load at all times.
  4. The pinion tip is 1.363 mm thick, more than the usual minimum of 0.25m.

15.09.title: Gear tooth strength
15.09.html:
A gear tooth can fail in two ways. It can break at the root, like a cantilever overloaded in bending fatigue. Or its working surface can pit: the repeated Hertz contact stress starts tiny subsurface cracks, as in a rolling bearing, and flakes come out of the flank. Each failure has its own classic formula, and both say the same thing about size: bigger teeth are stronger.

Bending: the Lewis equation

Wilfred Lewis (1892) treated the tooth as a cantilever loaded at its tip by the tangential force Wt​=2T/d. Fitting the largest parabola of uniform strength inside the tooth outline gives the critical section near the root and a dimensionless Lewis form factor Y that depends only on the tooth count and the profile:

σb​=FmYKv​Wt​​,Kv​=6.16.1+V​ (cut teeth, V in m/s).

F is the face width and m the module. Kv​, the Barth velocity factor, accounts for dynamic loads from small spacing errors, which grow with pitch-line speed V. Y rises from 0.245 at 12 teeth to 0.485 for a rack (more teeth means a wider root). Modern AGMA and ISO methods refine this with a computed geometry factor, overload and size factors, but the structure is the same.

Contact: Hertz on the flanks

Near the pitch point, two involute flanks act like two cylinders of radii ρi​=(di​/2)sinϕ pressed together by the normal load Wt​/cosϕ. Hertz line contact then gives the peak pressure. AGMA packages the geometry into a factor I:

σc​=Cp​Fd1​IKv​Wt​​​,I=2cosϕsinϕ​mG​+1mG​​,Cp​=π(E1​1−ν12​​+E2​1−ν22​​)1​​,

with gear ratio mG​=z2​/z1​. For steel on steel Cp​≈190 MPa​. The code checks that this formula is exactly the Hertz result for the two equivalent cylinders.

At fixed torque, a bigger module means a bigger pitch diameter, so a smaller Wt​; bending also gains the factor m in the denominator, so σb​∝1/m2 roughly, and σc​∝1/m. (The velocity factor grows a little with m, which slightly offsets the gain.)

Worked exampleSizing an 18 : 45 pair for 3 kW

Pinion 18 teeth at 1500 rpm, 3 kW, face width 20 mm, 20° pressure angle, steel (E=207 GPa, ν=0.3, so Cp​=190.3 MPa​).

  1. Torque 3000/(2π⋅25)=19.099 N·m.
  2. With m=2: d1​=36 mm, V=2.827 m/s, Wt​=2⋅19099/36=1061.0 N, Kv​=1.4635.
  3. Bending: Y(18)=0.309, so σb​=1.4635⋅1061.0/(20⋅2⋅0.309)=125.6 MPa.
  4. Contact: I=(cos20°sin20°/2)(2.5/3.5)=0.1148. The term under the root is 1.4635⋅1061.0/(20⋅36⋅0.1148)=18.79 MPa, so σc​=190.318.79​=824.8 MPa.
  5. Over modules 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3 and 4 mm, the bending stress is 205.7, 125.6, 86.8, 64.7 and 41.4 MPa and the contact stress 1055, 825, 685, 592 and 473 MPa. Both fall steadily.

Contact usually governs for hardened steel gears: 825 MPa needs a through-hardened or case-hardened steel, while 125.6 MPa in bending is modest.

Show step-by-step solution

  2. σc​∝1/F​: 824.820/25.13​=735.8 MPa.
  3. Face widths are usually kept between about 8 and 16 modules (16 to 32 mm here), so 25 mm is reasonable.

15.10.title: Planetary gear trains
15.10.html:
A planetary (epicyclic) gear set packs a large reduction into a small, coaxial package: a sun gear in the middle, several planets around it held by a carrier, and an internal ring gear outside. It is inside automatic car gearboxes, bicycle hub gears, e-bike hub motors and electric screwdrivers. Its trick is that it has two degrees of freedom: fix any one member (or drive two) and the third is determined.

The Willis equation

Watch the set from the carrier. In that rotating frame the carrier is still, so the gears form an ordinary train: sun to planet to ring, with an internal mesh that keeps the direction. The ratio is −zs​/zr​. Converting the relative speeds back to absolute ones gives the Willis equation:

ωs​−ωc​ωr​−ωc​​=−zr​zs​​.

Three common cases:

Fixed Input Output Ratio ωout​/ωin​
ring sun carrier zs​/(zs​+zr​)
sun carrier ring 1+zs​/zr​
sun ring carrier zr​/(zs​+zr​)

Locking any two members together locks the whole set: ratio 1.

Geometry and assembly. With one module, the ring must satisfy zr​=zs​+2zp​. Equally spaced planets fit only if (zs​+zr​)/N is a whole number, where N is the number of planets.

The code checks Willis independently: it solves the two rolling conditions (sun surface and ring surface move with the planet’s pitch points) for the planet spin and the unknown member.

Worked exampleA three-speed hub and an e-bike motor

  1. A bike hub gear with zs​=18, zp​=18, zr​=54 (54 = 18 + 2·18; (18 + 54)/3 = 24, so 3 or 4 planets fit, 5 do not).
  2. Sun locked to the axle. High gear: the sprocket drives the carrier, the ring drives the hub: 1+18/54=4/3, so the wheel turns 33.3% faster.
  3. Low gear: the sprocket drives the ring, the carrier drives the hub: 54/72=3/4, 25% slower. Direct: sprocket straight to the hub. These are the classic −25%, 0, +33% steps of a Sturmey-Archer AW-type hub, a total spread of (4/3)/(3/4)=1.778.
  4. The rolling-condition solver confirms, for example: with the sun still and the carrier at 1, the planets spin at 2 and the ring at 1.3333; with sun 2.5 and ring −1, the carrier turns at −0.125. Each case satisfies Willis to machine precision.
  5. An e-bike hub motor: motor on the sun (zs​=14), ring fixed (zr​=82, planets 34): the carrier turns 14/96 as fast, a reduction of 1+82/14=6.857:1.

Exercise 1A two-input case

In the 18-18-54 set, the sun turns at 300 rpm and the ring at 120 rpm in the same direction. How fast is the carrier, and how fast must the ring turn for the carrier to stand still?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Solve Willis for the carrier: ωc​=(ωr​+kωs​)/(1+k) with k=18/54=1/3.
  2. ωc​=(120+100)/(4/3)=165 rpm.
  3. Carrier still: ωr​/ωs​=−1/3, so the ring turns at −100 rpm, opposite to the sun. The set is then an ordinary train.

15.11.title: Belts and chains
15.11.html:
When two shafts are far apart, gears become heavy and expensive. A belt or a chain carries the power across the gap instead. Belts grip by friction and are quiet and forgiving; chains mesh positively with sprocket teeth and never slip. Each has one characteristic piece of physics: the belt’s capstan equation and the chain’s polygonal effect.

The polygonal effect

A chain is not a flexible band: it is a string of rigid links of pitch p, so it wraps the sprocket as a polygon, not a circle. The pitch radius of an N-tooth sprocket is

R=2sin(π/N)p​.

As the sprocket turns at ω, the straight span leaves from the pin at the top. While that pin swings through ±π/N around the top, the chain’s speed is ωRcosθ: it varies between ωRcos(π/N) and ωR once per tooth. The fractional speed fluctuation is

vmax​Δv​=1−cosNπ​≈2N2π2​.

It falls quickly with tooth count. That pulsing excites vibration and noise and adds dynamic load, which is why chain makers recommend at least 17 or so teeth on the small sprocket for fast drives. Bicycles get away with 11-tooth cogs because they turn slowly.

The capstan equation

A flat belt wrapped an angle θ around a pulley can hold a tension ratio of at most

T2​−Tc​T1​−Tc​​=eμθ,Tc​=m′v2,P=(T1​−T2​)v,

where T1​ is the tight side, T2​ the slack side, m′ the belt mass per metre and Tc​ the centrifugal tension, which the belt carries without contributing any grip. A V-belt wedges into a groove of angle 2β, multiplying the effective friction to μ′=μ/sinβ: with a 40° groove, almost three times more. That is why the CVT in a scooter uses a V-belt.

Assumptions: the chain span leaves horizontally from the top pin (no span vibration), the belt is inextensible and slips everywhere at once at the limit (real belts creep over part of the arc).

Worked exampleBike sprockets and a scooter belt

  1. Bicycle chain, pitch 12.7 mm. An 11-tooth cog has pitch radius 22.539 mm; simulating the top pin over two tooth periods gives a speed fluctuation of 4.051%, matching 1−cos(π/11).
  2. For 14, 18, 25, 32 and 42 teeth: 2.507%, 1.519%, 0.789%, 0.482% and 0.280%. A big chainring runs almost smoothly.
  3. A flat belt carries 2 kW at 12 m/s with μ=0.35 over 160° of wrap; it weighs 0.12 kg/m. Then eμθ=2.6575, Tc​=0.12⋅144=17.28 N and T1​−T2​=2000/12=166.7 N.
  4. Slack side T2​=166.7/(2.6575−1)+17.28=117.8 N, tight side 284.5 N, so the belt must be installed with an initial tension of about (T1​+T2​)/2=201.2 N.
  5. A V-belt in a 40° groove has μ′=0.35/sin20°=1.023 and eμ′θ=17.42.

  2. 1−cos(π/16)=0.01921, about 1.92%. The approximation π2/(2⋅256)=1.93% is close.
  3. e0.3π=2.566 (ignoring centrifugal tension).

15.12.title: Bolted joints and preload
15.12.html:
A bolt is a spring. Tighten it and it stretches a little while the parts it clamps squeeze a little. That preload is the whole point: a well-preloaded joint carries most of an external pulling load by unloading the clamped parts, not by loading the bolt. This is why a correctly torqued bolt survives fatigue loads that would snap a loose one.

Stiffness of the bolt and the members

Inside the grip length l, the bolt is an unthreaded shank of area Ad​ and length ld​ in series with a threaded part of tensile stress area At​ and length lt​:

kb​=Ad​lt​+At​ld​Ad​At​E​.

The clamped members are compressed in a region that spreads out from the washer face roughly as a 30° cone (a frustum). For two equal steel members with a washer face of 1.5d, integrating that cone gives

km​=2ln(50.5774l+2.5d0.5774l+0.5d​)0.5774πEd​.

The members are typically three to five times stiffer than the bolt.

The joint diagram

Preload Fi​ stretches the bolt and compresses the members. An external load P pulling the joint apart stretches both by the same extra amount δ, so the bolt gains kb​δ and the members lose km​δ, with kb​δ+km​δ=P:

Fb​=Fi​+CP,Fm​=Fi​−(1−C)P,C=kb​+km​kb​​.

C is the joint constant, usually 0.15 to 0.3: the bolt feels only a fraction of the load. This holds until the members' compression reaches zero at the separation load P0​=Fi​/(1−C); beyond it, the joint opens and the bolt takes everything. Typical preload is 75% of the bolt’s proof load for reusable joints and 90% for permanent ones, applied with a tightening torque T≈KFi​d, where the nut factor K≈0.2 for dry steel (and scatters by ±25%, which is why critical joints use angle or stretch control).

Worked exampleAn M10 class 8.8 bolt through two steel plates

d=10 mm, At​=58.0 mm², proof strength 600 MPa; two 15 mm plates (grip 30 mm); a 40 mm long bolt with threaded length 2d+6=26 mm, so ld​=14 mm and lt​=16 mm in the grip.

  1. kb​=78.54⋅58.0⋅207000/(78.54⋅16+58.0⋅14)=455.8 kN/mm.
  2. km​=0.5774π⋅207000⋅10/(2ln(5⋅22.32/42.32))=1936.1 kN/mm.
  3. C=455.8/(455.8+1936.1)=0.1906.
  4. Preload 0.75⋅58.0⋅600=26.10 kN, from a torque of about 0.2⋅26100⋅0.010=52.2 N·m.
  5. Simulating the bolt and plates as two springs: at P=15 kN the bolt carries 28.959 kN (it gained only 2.859 kN = C⋅15) and the plates still press with 13.959 kN. Bolt stress 499.3 MPa, below the 600 MPa proof.
  6. Separation at P0​=26.10/(1−0.1906)=32.24 kN. At 40 kN the joint is open and the bolt carries all 40 kN.

Exercise 1A fatigue load

The same joint sees an external load cycling between 0 and 10 kN. What is the bolt force range, and what would it be without any preload?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. With preload: from Fi​=26.10 kN to 26.10+0.1906⋅10=28.01 kN. The alternating force is only ±0.95 kN.
  2. Without preload the joint is open from the start: the bolt goes from 0 to 10 kN, an alternating force of ±5 kN, more than five times larger.
  3. Preload trades a higher mean stress for a much smaller alternating stress, and alternating stress is what drives fatigue.

15.13.title: Welded joints
15.13.html:
Most steel structures, from bicycle frames to trailer hitches, are held together by welds. The commonest is the fillet weld: a triangular bead laid in the corner between two plates. It is analysed with a simple and deliberately conservative idea: whatever the actual load direction, treat the stress on the weld’s narrowest section, the throat, as shear.

The throat and the weld as a line

A fillet weld with equal legs h has a throat t=hcos45°=0.707h. A weld of length L carrying a force F along it has an average throat shear stress

τ=0.707hLF​.

For a group of welds loaded eccentrically, treat each weld as a line and use the same steps as a bolt group:

  1. Find the centroid of the weld lines.
  2. Direct shear: τ′=F/A with A=0.707h∑Li​, in the direction of the load.
  3. Torsional shear: the moment M=Fe about the centroid gives τ′′=Mr/J, perpendicular to the radius r, with J=0.707hJu​ and Ju​ the unit polar moment of the lines. For two parallel lines of length b a distance d apart, Ju​=b(3d2+b2)/6.
  4. Add the two vectorially and find the largest magnitude, usually at the point farthest from the centroid.

Every stress scales as 1/h, so the leg size follows directly from an allowable stress. A common static allowable is τall​=0.3Sut​ of the electrode (AISC), for example 0.3⋅482=145 MPa for an E70 electrode.

Assumptions: the base metal is stronger than the weld, stresses spread uniformly along each line, and residual stresses and fatigue are ignored. Fatigue is where welds really fail: the toe of a weld is a severe notch, and fatigue design uses separate detail categories.

Worked exampleA trailer hitch bracket

A plate is welded to a post with two horizontal fillet welds, each 50 mm long and 80 mm apart. A load of 10 kN acts downwards 150 mm from the centroid of the welds.

  1. Ju​=50(3⋅802+502)/6=180833 mm³. With h=6 mm: t=4.242 mm, A=4.242⋅100=424.2 mm², J=767095 mm⁴.
  2. Direct shear 10000/424.2=23.57 MPa, downwards.
  3. M=10000⋅150=1.5×106 N·mm. At the far corner (25,40) mm from the centroid: horizontal torsional component 1.5×106⋅40/767095=78.22 MPa, vertical 1.5×106⋅25/767095=48.89 MPa.
  4. Resultant 78.222+(23.57+48.89)2​=106.6 MPa. Summing 8000 small weld elements gives the same value and the same location.
  5. With h = 4, 6 and 8 mm the stress is 159.9, 106.6 and 80.0 MPa: exactly 1/h. For 145 MPa the leg must be at least 4⋅159.9/145=4.41 mm, so specify 5 mm.

A 10 mm thick bar is joined to a plate by two side fillet welds, 6 mm leg, each 80 mm long, carrying 120 kN along the welds. What is the throat shear stress? What length of each weld would bring it to 145 MPa?

  2. τ=120000/678.7=176.8 MPa, too high.
  3. Required total length 120000/(0.707⋅6⋅145)=195.1 mm, so about 98 mm per weld; round up to 100 mm.

15.14.title: Helical springs
15.14.html:
A helical compression spring looks like a bending problem, but it is really a torsion bar wound into a helix. Push on the ends and every section of the wire twists by the same torque, T=FD/2. That one observation gives the spring rate and the stress.

Rate and stress

A spring with wire diameter d, mean coil diameter D and n active coils has a wire length of about πDn. Twisting it by T=FD/2 rotates one end of the wire relative to the other by θ=TL/(GJ), and that rotation moves the load point by θD/2. With J=πd4/32:

k=δF​=8D3nGd4​.

The rate goes as d4 and 1/D3, so small changes in wire or coil size matter a lot, and it is inversely proportional to the number of coils: twice the coils, half the rate.

The maximum shear stress is the torsion stress 8FD/(πd3), increased by the curvature of the wire (the inside of the coil is shorter, so it is more strained) and by the direct shear of F. The Wahl factor combines both, with spring index C=D/d:

τ=KW​πd38FD​,KW​=4C−44C−1​+C0.615​.

Practical springs have C between 4 and 12. Spring wire is very strong and gets stronger as it gets thinner, roughly Sut​=A/dm; for oil-tempered wire A=1855 MPa·mmm and m=0.187, and the torsional yield strength is about 0.50Sut​.

The code checks the rate formula independently: it builds the actual helix, computes the moment of the load at each wire section, splits it into torsion and bending, and integrates the strain energy. For a pitch of 1.6 wire diameters, the helix angle adds a tiny bending share and the result is 0.11% softer than the formula.

Worked exampleA scooter suspension spring

Oil-tempered wire d=5 mm, mean diameter D=40 mm, 8 active coils, G=79.3 GPa.

  1. k=79300⋅54/(8⋅403⋅8)=12.100 N/mm. The helix strain-energy integral gives 12.087 N/mm (−0.11%).
  2. With 6, 10 or 12 coils: 16.134, 9.680 and 8.067 N/mm.
  3. Under 600 N (rider weight share plus a bump): deflection 600/12.10=49.6 mm.
  4. C=8, KW​=31/28+0.615/8=1.1840, so τ=1.1840⋅8⋅600⋅40/(π⋅125)=578.9 MPa.
  5. Sut​=1855/50.187=1373 MPa, Ssy​=686 MPa: a static factor of 1.19. Thin for a part that is hammered by potholes; a fatigue check would push towards thicker wire or a larger diameter.

15.15.title: Clutches and brakes
15.15.html:
A brake and a clutch are the same device used two ways: two surfaces pressed together so that friction carries a torque. A bicycle disc brake converts the bike’s kinetic energy into heat in the rotor; a car clutch connects a spinning engine to a stationary gearbox. The design question is the same for both: how much torque does a given clamping force produce?

Friction torque on an annulus

A friction face between radii ri​ and ro​ carries a contact pressure p(r). The clamp force and the torque are

F=∫ri​ro​​p2πrdr,T=∫ri​ro​​μpr2πrdr.

The answer depends on how the pressure is distributed, and there are two classic assumptions:

  1. Uniform pressure (new, perfectly flat, rigid surfaces): p is constant, and
T=32​μFro2​−ri2​ro3​−ri3​​.
  1. Uniform wear (after running in): wear is proportional to pressure times sliding speed, and speed is proportional to r. Faces that stay flat wear equally everywhere only if pr is constant, so the outer region carries less pressure. Then
T=μF2ro​+ri​​.

Uniform wear always gives the smaller torque, because it shifts pressure inwards to smaller radii. Designers use it because it is the conservative, long-term value. The difference is small for narrow faces (ri​/ro​ near 1) and grows for wide ones. A clutch with several plates multiplies the torque by the number of friction faces. A disc brake has two faces, one on each side of the rotor. A pad covers only a sector of the annulus, but the sector angle cancels from both formulas.

Hydraulic actuation. The lever multiplies the hand force, and the hydraulic system multiplies it again by the ratio of piston areas: Fpad​=Fhand​⋅(lever ratio)⋅Acaliper​/Amaster​.

Worked exampleA hydraulic bicycle disc brake

160 mm rotor with pads from 62 to 78 mm radius; 100 N at the lever, 4 : 1 lever ratio, 10 mm master piston, two 22 mm caliper pistons on each side; resin pads with μ=0.40.

  1. Line pressure 400/(π⋅102/4)=5.093 MPa; clamp force per side 5.093⋅2⋅380.1=3872.0 N.
  2. Uniform wear: T=2⋅0.40⋅3872.0⋅0.070=216.83 N·m (two faces, mean radius 70 mm).
  3. Uniform pressure: effective radius 32​(783−623)/(782−622)=70.30 mm, so T=217.78 N·m. Numerical integration of both pressure laws matches to six figures.
  4. At the tyre (radius 0.35 m): 216.83/0.35=620 N, a deceleration of 6.88 m/s² for 90 kg. That is close to the limit at which the rear wheel lifts, so a front brake never needs more.
  5. Stopping from 40 km/h dissipates 21​⋅90⋅11.112=5.56 kJ, mostly in the small steel rotor. That heat is why long descents fade brakes.

Exercise 1A car clutch

A single-plate dry clutch has friction faces from 75 to 120 mm radius, a spring force of 4 kN and μ=0.3, with two faces. Find the torque capacity under both assumptions.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Uniform wear: T=2⋅0.3⋅4000⋅(0.120+0.075)/2=234.0 N·m.
  2. Uniform pressure: effective radius 32​(1203−753)/(1202−752)=99.23 mm, so T=2⋅0.3⋅4000⋅0.09923=238.2 N·m.
  3. Design on 234 N·m. The wider face makes the difference larger than on the brake pad (1.8% here, against 0.4%).

15.16.title: Linkage synthesis
15.16.html:
Analysis asks: given a linkage, how does it move? Synthesis asks the reverse: given the motion I want, what linkage produces it? For the four-bar linkage there is a remarkably neat answer when the goal is a function generator, where the output rocker angle ψ must follow the input crank angle ϕ at chosen points.

The Freudenstein equation

Put the ground pivots at the origin and at (d,0). The crank of length a ends at A=a(cosϕ,sinϕ); the rocker of length c ends at B=(d,0)+c(cosψ,sinψ). The coupler is rigid, ∣B−A∣=b. Expanding the square and dividing by 2ac gives the Freudenstein equation:

K1​cosψ−K2​cosϕ+K3​=cos(ϕ−ψ),K1​=ad​,  K2​=cd​,  K3​=2aca2−b2+c2+d2​.

It is linear in the three unknowns K1​,K2​,K3​. So three desired pairs (ϕj​,ψj​), the precision points, give a 3 × 3 linear system. Solve it, and the link lengths follow: a=d/K1​, c=d/K2​, b2=a2+c2+d2−2acK3​. The ground length d just sets the scale.

Three warnings, all checked in the code:

  1. A negative a or c means that link points the other way; a negative b2 means no linkage exists. Choose different precision points.
  2. A four-bar has two assembly branches (open and crossed). The synthesized linkage passes the precision points on one of them only, and it cannot jump between branches without being taken apart.
  3. Between the precision points the function is only approximated. Spacing the points well (Chebyshev spacing) minimises the error.

The Grashof condition s+l≤p+q (shortest plus longest at most the sum of the other two) tells you whether some link can rotate fully. With the shortest link as the crank, the result is a crank-rocker, like a windscreen-wiper drive.

Worked exampleA wiper-style drive

Targets: crank at 40°, 70°, 100° should put the rocker at 70°, 80°, 95°. Ground d=100 mm.

  1. The linear system gives K1​=2.3744, K2​=1.2230, K3​=0.9908.
  2. So a=100/2.3744=42.115 mm, c=100/1.2230=81.768 mm, and b=107.870 mm.
  3. Solving the assembled linkage by circle intersection gives exactly 70.000000°, 80.000000° and 95.000000° at the three crank angles on one branch; the other branch misses by more than 2 rad.
  4. Grashof: 42.1+107.9=150.0≤81.8+100=181.8, and the crank is the shortest link, so it can turn fully. Over a full turn the rocker swings between 69.19° and 139.11°.

Exercise 1Check a design by hand

With a=42.115, b=107.870, c=81.768 and d=100 mm, verify the Freudenstein equation at ϕ=70°, ψ=80°.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. K1​=2.3744, K2​=1.2230, K3​=(42.1152−107.8702+81.7682+1002)/(2⋅42.115⋅81.768)=0.9908.
  2. Left side: 2.3744cos80°−1.2230cos70°+0.9908=0.4123−0.4183+0.9908=0.9848.
  3. Right side: cos(70°−80°)=cos10°=0.9848. They agree.

15.17.title: "Case study: a ski-lift grip"
15.17.html:
A detachable chairlift lets chairs crawl slowly through the stations for boarding and then race up the mountain at 5 m/s. At the station exit each chair’s grip clamps onto the moving haul rope; at the top it lets go again. Nothing but friction holds a chair full of people to a steel rope on a steep slope. This case study puts several Phase 15 tools together: friction, springs, safety factors and belt-drive tension. It is an educational model: real grips are designed and tested to standards such as EN 13796, with values and procedures that differ in detail from the ones used here.

Will the grip slip?

A grip squeezes the rope between jaws with a clamping force Fc​ from a stack of springs. With friction coefficient μ on each of two jaw faces, the largest force along the rope it can resist is

Fgrip​=2μFc​.

On a rope inclined at θ, a loaded chair of mass m pulls downhill along the rope with mgsinθ. Requiring a safety factor SF against slipping:

2μFc​ ≥ SF⋅mgsinθ⟺θ≤θmax​=arcsinSFmg2μFc​​.

The steepest point of the line is usually just after a tower, where the rope bends. Grips are checked at every station pass with a force-testing device, because worn jaws or tired springs reduce Fc​, and with it the margin.

Rope tension and the drive

The rope is kept taut by a tensioning weight (or hydraulic ram) at one terminal, which sets the bottom tension T0​. Climbing a height H, the tension rises by the weight per metre times H (friction ignored):

Ttop​=T0​+(mrope′​+smchair​​)gH,

with chairs every s metres. The uphill side carries loaded chairs, the downhill side empty ones, so the uphill top tension is larger. The bullwheel at the drive terminal transmits the difference by friction, exactly like a belt pulley, so the capstan equation Tup​/Tdown​≤eμπ must hold. The drive power is (Tup​−Tdown​)v.

Worked exampleA detachable quad chair

Chair 250 kg plus four riders of 100 kg: m=650 kg. Grip clamping force 35 kN, μ=0.20, SF=3.

  1. At a 45° rope angle the downhill pull is 650⋅9.81⋅sin45°=4509 N, so the required capacity is 13 527 N.
  2. Grip capacity 2⋅0.20⋅35000=14000 N: it holds, just. The steepest angle with SF=3 is arcsin(14000/19130)=47.04°.
  3. The code checks over 179 rope angles that “holds” is exactly “capacity ≥ slope component × SF”. For 45° the clamp force must be at least 33.82 kN.
  4. Line: 400 m vertical, rope 6.5 kg/m, chairs every 20 m, T0​=200 kN. Uphill top tension 200+(6.5+32.5)⋅9.81⋅400/1000=353.0 kN; downhill, with empty chairs, 274.6 kN.
  5. Ratio 1.286, below the bullwheel’s limit e0.25π=2.193: no slip. Drive power 78.5 kN⋅5 m/s=392 kW, before friction. A rope with a 1.6 MN breaking load has a factor of 4.53.

Exercise 1Worn jaws

After a season the jaw friction drops to μ=0.15. What is the steepest rope angle the same grip can hold with SF=3? What clamping force would restore 45°?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. θmax​=arcsin(2⋅0.15⋅35000/(3⋅650⋅9.81))=arcsin(0.5489)=33.29°.
  2. For 45°: Fc​=13527/(2⋅0.15)=45.09 kN.
  3. That sensitivity is why grip force is tested daily and jaws are replaced on schedule.

15.18.title: "Design review: a calculation report from code"
15.18.html:
A design is not finished when the numbers work out on your screen. Someone else has to check it: a colleague, a customer, a certification body. A design review walks through every requirement, the calculation behind it and its margin. The best way to make that review trustworthy is to generate the calculation report directly from the code that does the calculations, so the report can never drift away from the analysis.

What a calculation report contains

  1. Inputs: loads, speeds, materials, geometry, with sources.
  2. Checks: each failure mode with its value, its limit and a pass or fail status.
  3. Assumptions: what the models leave out (Phase 15 has listed them in every lesson).
  4. Result: a single line saying whether everything passes, and which checks govern.

When an input changes (a heavier load, a cheaper bearing), you rerun the script and the whole report updates. Version control then records which report belongs to which design.

Report from code, and a test that it is right

The code below gathers checks from this phase for the countershaft of lesson 15.04: peak bending moment, endurance limit, DE-Goodman safety factor, bearing L10 lives at both supports (lesson 15.06), and key shear and crushing (lesson 15.05). It writes a Markdown table, which renders on GitHub or converts to PDF. Then it parses the report back and checks that every printed number matches the computed value to the printed precision, and that every status is right. A second run with a thinner shaft must show a failure.

This is the same idea as an automated test in software: the report is an output that can be checked by a machine, not only read by a person.

Worked exampleThe countershaft report

Inputs as in lesson 15.04: 150 N·m at 600 rpm; gear 2000 N at 100 mm and pulley 1200 N at 220 mm on a 300 mm span; 1045 steel; bearings with C=19.5 kN (about a 6206); a 10 × 8 × 40 mm key in 1018 steel (Sy​=370 MPa) with a design factor of 2.

Check Value Limit Status
Peak bending moment 165.33 N·m info
Endurance limit Se​ 220.31 MPa info
Fatigue factor (DE-Goodman), d=32 mm 2.03 ≥ 2.00 pass
Bearing L10, left 45 574 h ≥ 20 000 h pass
Bearing L10, right 55 669 h ≥ 20 000 h pass
Key shear 23.44 MPa ≤ 106.74 MPa pass
Key crushing 58.59 MPa ≤ 185.00 MPa pass
  1. The left bearing carries R1​=1653.3 N: L10​=(19500/1653.3)3=1640.7 million revolutions, or 45 574 h at 600 rpm.
  2. Key shear 2⋅150000/(32⋅10⋅40)=23.44 MPa.
  3. The parser reads all seven rows back and every value and status agrees.
  4. With a 28 mm shaft the fatigue factor falls to 1.375 and the report says “1 check(s) fail”. The governing check is shaft fatigue; the bearings and key have large margins.

Exercise 1Adding a check

Add a static yield check for the shaft: the peak von Mises stress (32Kf​M/πd3)2+3(16Kfs​T/πd3)2​ must be at most Sy​/1.5 with Sy​=530 MPa. Compute it for d=32 mm.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Bending 32⋅1.7⋅165333/(π⋅323)=87.37 MPa.
  2. Torsion 16⋅1.5⋅150000/(π⋅323)=34.97 MPa, so 3​⋅34.97=60.57 MPa.
  3. von Mises 87.372+60.572​=106.3 MPa against a limit of 530/1.5=353.3 MPa: pass, with a big margin. Fatigue governs, as usual for rotating shafts.
  4. In code: one more tuple in the checks list, and the parser test covers it automatically.
